items.english_text: Having conceived the unoriginate Word of God the Father, by thy maternal boldness diligently pray, O Mother of God, that He may settle Thy servants where the choir of the righteous unceasingly makes merry and praises thee, where there is eternal brightness and the sweet voice of those who keep festival![^1369]

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: By the prayers of all the saints, O Lord, and of the Theotokos, grant us Thy peace, and have mercy on us, as the only Compassionate One!

provenance.verbatim_source: By the prayers of all the saints, O Lord, and of the Theotokos, grant us Thy peace, and have mercy on us, as the only Compassionate One!

items.english_text: Your confession at the judgment seat, O holy ones, spat upon the power of demons, and delivered mankind from deceit; therefore even as your heads were being cut off, ye cried aloud: "Let the sacrifice of our souls be acceptable before Thee, O Lord, for having loved Thee, we took no heed of temporal life, O Lover of mankind!"

items.english_text: O what a good merchandise is yours, O holy ones! For ye gave blood and inherited the heavens; and having been tested for a time, ye rejoice eternally; truly good is your merchandise; for leaving behind corruptible things, ye received the incorruptible,[^1371] and dancing with the Angels, ye unceasingly sing unto the Consubstantial Trinity!

items.english_text: O all-praised martyrs, neither did the earth hide you, but heaven received you, and the gates of Paradise were opened unto you; and being within, ye enjoy the Tree of Life;[^1372] pray unto Christ that He grant peace and great mercy unto our souls!

items.english_text: What earthly sweetness remains without part in grief? What glory stands immutable upon the earth? All things are more feeble than shadows, and all things are more deceitful than dreams; in a single hour death takes all these things away; but in the light of Thy countenance, O Christ, and in the enjoyment of Thy beauty, give rest unto those whom Thou hast chosen, as the Lover of mankind![^1373]

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: The world's glory, who sprouted forth from mankind and gave birth unto the Master, the heavenly gate, let us hymn: Mary the Virgin, the song of the bodiless powers and the adornment of the faithful; for she was shown to be heaven and the temple of the Godhead; she, having broken down the barrier of enmity, brought in peace and opened the Kingdom; having her therefore as the confirmation of our faith, we have as our champion the Lord born of her; take courage therefore, take courage, O people of God, for He will conquer the enemies, as Almighty![^1374]

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.slavonic_text: Земны́хъ наслажде́нїй не возлюби́вше страстоте́рпцы, небе́сныхъ благи́хъ сподо́бишасѧ, и҆ А҆́гг҃лѡвъ согражда́не бы́ша, Гдⷭ҇и моли́твами и҆́хъ поми́лꙋй, и҆ спасѝ на́съ.
items.english_text: Not having loved earthly delights, the passion-bearers were counted worthy of heavenly good things, and became fellow citizens of the Angels; O Lord, by their prayers have mercy and save us!

provenance.verbatim_source: Not having loved earthly delights, the passion-bearers were counted worthy of heavenly good things, and became fellow citizens of the Angels; O Lord, by their prayers have mercy and save us!

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.slavonic_text: Ст҃ы̑мъ мꙋ́ченикѡмъ молѧ́щымсѧ ѡ҆ на́съ, и҆ Хрⷭ҇та̀ пою́щымъ, всѧ́ка пре́лесть преста̀, и҆ человѣ́ческїй ро́дъ вѣ́рою спаса́етсѧ.
items.english_text: While the holy martyrs pray for us and hymn Christ, all deceit hath ceased, and the human race is saved by faith.

provenance.verbatim_source: While the holy martyrs pray for us and hymn Christ, all deceit hath ceased, and the human race is saved by faith.

items.slavonic_text: Ли́цы мꙋ́ченичестїи проти́вишасѧ мꙋчи́телемъ, глаго́люще: мы̀ во́инствꙋемъ Царю̀ си́лъ, а́ще и҆ ѻ҆гню̀, и҆ мꙋ́камъ предади́те на́съ, не ѿмета́емся Трⷪ҇ческїѧ си́лы.
items.english_text: The choirs of the martyrs resisted the tormentors, saying: "We serve as soldiers for the King of hosts; even though ye hand us over unto fire and torments, we do not deny the power of the Trinity!"

provenance.verbatim_source: The choirs of the martyrs resisted the tormentors, saying: "We serve as soldiers for the King of hosts; even though ye hand us over unto fire and torments, we do not deny the power of the Trinity!"

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.slavonic_text: Ве́лїа сла́ва, ю҆́же стѧжа́сте ст҃і́и вѣ́рою: не то́кмѡ бо въ страда́нїихъ врага̀ побѣди́ли є҆стѐ, но и҆ по сме́рти дꙋ́хи прого́ните, недꙋ́жныѧ и҆сцѣля́ете, дꙋ́шъ и҆ тѣле́съ вра́чеве моли́теся ко Гдⷭ҇ꙋ, поми́ловатися дꙋша́мъ на́шымъ.
items.english_text: Great is the glory which ye acquired through faith, O holy ones! For not only in sufferings did ye conquer the enemy, but even after death ye drive away evil spirits, and heal the infirm; O physicians of souls and bodies, pray unto the Lord that our souls may find mercy!

items.slavonic_text: Оу҆вы̀ мнѣ̀! коли́къ по́двигъ и҆́мать дꙋша̀ разлꙋча́ющися ѿ тѣлесѐ; ᲂу҆вы̀ мнѣ̀! тогда̀ коли́кѡ слези́тъ, и҆ нѣ́сть и҆́же поми́лꙋетъ ю҆̀: ко А҆́гг҃лѡмъ ѻ҆́чи возводя́щи, бездѣ́льнѡ мо́лится: къ человѣ́кѡмъ рꙋ́цѣ простира́ющи, и҆ не и҆́мать помога́ющагѡ, тѣ́мже возлю́бленнаѧ моѧ̀ бра́тїе, разꙋмѣ́вше кра́ткꙋю на́шꙋ жи́знь, преста́вленнымъ поко́й ѿ Хрⷭ҇та̀ про́симъ, и҆ дꙋша́мъ на́шымъ ве́лїю ми́лость.
items.english_text: Woe is me! What a struggle hath the soul when parting from the body! Woe is me! How much she weeps then, and there is none that hath mercy upon her! Raising her eyes unto the Angels, she prays in vain; stretching out her hands unto men, she hath none to help; therefore, my beloved brethren, understanding our brief life, let us ask of Christ rest for the departed, and great mercy for our souls![^1376]

items.slavonic_text: Пре́йде сѣ́нь зако́ннаѧ, бл҃года́ти прише́дшей, ꙗ҆́коже бо кꙋпина̀ не сгара́ше ѡ҆пала́ема, та́кѡ Дв҃а родила̀ є҆сѝ, и҆ Дв҃а пребыла̀ є҆сѝ, вмѣ́стѡ столпа̀ ѻ҆́гненнагѡ пра́ведное возсїѧ̀ Со́лнце: вмѣ́стѡ Мѡѷсе́а Хрⷭ҇то́съ спасе́нїе дꙋ́шъ на́шихъ.
items.english_text: The shadow of the Law passed away when grace arrived; for as the bush was not consumed when burning, so as a Virgin didst thou give birth, and a Virgin didst thou remain; instead of a pillar of fire, the righteous Sun hath shone forth; instead of Moses, Christ, the salvation of our souls![^1377]

items.english_text: It is good to conceal the secret of a king, but it is glorious to proclaim the works of God! For so said the Angel unto Tobit, after the glorious restoration of his sight following his blindness.[^1379] For not to keep the secrets of a king is perilous and a cause of stumbling, whereas to pass over in silence the all-glorious works of God brings peril unto the soul. Therefore, I also fear to keep silent concerning the works of God, remembering the punishment of that servant who received the Lord's talent and hid it in the earth, and made no gain therewith.[^1380] Having heard a sacred narrative, I can in no wise conceal it; and let none of you disbelieve me upon hearing these writings, nor think that I speak in pride while marveling at this great miracle; far be it from me to speak falsely concerning holy things! And if there be certain persons who read these books and, marveling at the loftiness of the account, refuse to believe, may the mercy of the Lord be upon them; for they, considering only human weakness, count as unacceptable the things spoken by us concerning men. Now, therefore, it is fitting for me to begin this narrative and most marvelous event which took place in our generation.

items.english_text: There was a certain elder in one of the monasteries of Palestine, adorned in manner of life and in word, raised from his very swaddling clothes in monastic customs, and faithful; and the name of that elder was Zosimas. And let no one suppose that this man was that Zosimas the heretic, even though the two shared a single common name;[^1381] for this righteous Zosimas practiced every form of fasting and ascetic labor, and kept all the traditions, and while doing all this, that elder never grew slack in the meditation of the divine words; whether lying down or rising up, holding his work in his hands or partaking of food—if indeed one ought to call food that of which the elder partook—he had one unceasing work, which was to chant psalms continually. For from his very infancy he had been entrusted to the monastery, and he completed up to his fiftieth year therein.

provenance.verbatim_source: There was a certain elder in one of the monasteries of Palestine, adorned in manner of life and in word, raised from his very swaddling clothes in monastic customs, and faithful; and the name of that elder was Zosimas. And let no one suppose that this man was that Zosimas the heretic, even though the two shared a single common name;[^1381] for this righteous Zosimas practiced every form of fasting and ascetic labor, and kept all the traditions, and while doing all this, that elder never grew slack in the meditation of the divine words; whether lying down or rising up, holding his work in his hands or partaking of food—if indeed one ought to call food that of which the elder partook—he had one unceasing work, which was to chant psalms continually. For from his very infancy he had been entrusted to the monastery, and he completed up to his fiftieth year therein.

items.english_text: And while that elder was living thus in the monastery, he reasoned within himself, saying: "Is there then a monk upon the earth who can show me a form of ascetic life which I have not accomplished? Can a man be found in the wilderness who surpasses me in deed?" And as the elder pondered thus, an Angel appeared unto him and said: "O Zosimas, nobly indeed hast thou struggled so far as a man is able, yet no man is perfect. But that thou mayest understand how many other ways of salvation there are, go forth out of thy land, like Abraham out of the house of his father,[^1382] and go unto the monastery that lies beside the Jordan."

items.english_text: Immediately the elder went forth from his monastery, and followed the one speaking unto him; and being led by the will of God, he arrived at the monastery beside the Jordan. And having knocked at the gate, word was brought to the abbot; and entering in, Zosimas made a prostration according to the monastic custom. And the abbot questioned him: "Whence art thou, brother, and for what cause hast thou come unto us poor old men?" Zosimas answered: "Inquire not of me whence I have come; but I have come for the sake of spiritual profit, for I have heard of your great and praiseworthy rule, which is able to lead souls unto Christ our God." And the abbot said unto him: "God alone, O brother, Who heals the human race—may He Himself teach both thee and us His will, and guide thee to perform all things that are profitable."

items.english_text: And when the abbot had spoken these things unto Zosimas, the elder bowed down, offered a prayer, saying "Amen," and remained in that monastery. And he beheld there monks shining in actions and deeds, and fervent in spirit; their chanting was unceasing, their standing lasted all through the night, manual labor was ever in their hands, and psalms were in their mouths; there was no idle word among them, and their sole care was to count themselves dead in body; their nourishment was the words of God, and they sustained the body with bread and water. Seeing these things, Zosimas marveled, and strove eagerly toward the course set before him.

items.english_text: And when many days had passed, the season of the Holy and Great Fast drew near; the gates of the monastery were kept locked and were never opened, save only when one of the brethren went out for some necessity, for the place was solitary, and not only untrodden, but unknown to people of the world. Now this was the rule handed down in that monastery, for the sake of which God had brought Zosimas thither: On the First Sunday of the Fast, the presbyter celebrated the Divine Liturgy, and all partook of the Most Pure Body and Blood of Christ our God, and tasted a little food; afterward they gathered in the church, and having offered lengthy prayer and genuflections, the elders kissed one another and the abbot, and having received a blessing, they opened the monastery gates, chanting in unison: "The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"[^1383] And chanting the rest of that psalm, they all went forth, leaving one or two brethren behind—not to guard the monastery, for there was nothing therein to be stolen by thieves, but so that the church might not remain without divine service.

items.english_text: And each carried provisions for himself, according as each was able and wished: one took a little bread, another figs, another dates, another pulse soaked in water, and another nothing at all save his own body and the ragged garments which he wore; and whenever their body was in need, they fed upon the herbs and plants of the wilderness. Thus they crossed the Jordan and separated far from one another, and none knew how his neighbor fasted or how he labored in asceticism. And if anyone happened to catch sight of his brother walking toward him, he immediately turned aside in another direction, and lived alone by himself, chanting continually unto God.

items.english_text: After walking for seven days, he halted a little from his journey, praying at the time of the sixth hour, and turning toward the east, he offered the customary prayers; for he used to pause a little from his journey and rest at each canonical hour, chanting and making prostrations. And while he stood chanting, he saw to his right side a shadow, as if of a human body; at first he was afraid, supposing it to be a demonic apparition, and trembling, he signed himself with the sign of the Cross; and having cast off fear, he remained without dread, for he was already concluding his prayer. Turning then his eyes toward the south, he saw someone walking, unclothed in body, and darkened in appearance from the burning of the sun; and the hair upon her head was white as wool, and short, reaching only down to the neck.

items.english_text: Seeing this, Zosimas rejoiced over that remarkable sight, and began to run in the direction where he saw the figure, rejoicing with great joy; for during all those days he had seen no human form, nor bird, nor beast, nor creeping thing. When that figure saw Zosimas approaching from afar, she began to run and flee into the inner wilderness. And Zosimas, as if forgetting his old age and the fatigue of his journey, ran swiftly, wishing to overtake the one fleeing. He pursued, and she fled; yet swifter was the running of Zosimas than of the one fleeing. And when he drew near enough that his voice could be heard, Zosimas began to cry aloud with tears in these words: "Why dost thou flee from me, a sinful old man, O servant of the true God, for Whose sake thou dwellest in this wilderness? Wait for me, who am sinful and unworthy and weak! Halt, and bestow upon me, an old man, thy prayer and blessing, for the sake of God, Who never rejects anyone!"

items.english_text: While Zosimas spoke these things with tears, they were running near to one another and came to a dry torrent bed—though I do not think a torrent ever flowed there. When she reached that place, the fleeing one descended to the other side; and Zosimas, exhausted by old age and unable to run any further, stood on his side of the torrent bed, and added tears unto tears, and lamentation unto lamentation. Then the fleeing figure called out with a voice unto him, saying: "Abba Zosimas, I cannot turn and show myself before thy face, for I am a woman without clothing, as thou seest; but if thou wishest to bestow thy prayer upon me, a sinful woman, cast me the cloak which thou wearest, that I may cover my feminine weakness, and turn toward thee, and receive thy prayer."

And he quickly did as he had been told, and taking off the old and tattered cloak which he wore, he cast it toward her while turning his face away. And as the elder lay upon the ground, a troubled thought entered his mind, wondering whether she might be a spirit pretending to prayin order to deceive him. items.english_text: Hearing and seeing these things, the elder fell at her feet, saying with tears: "I adjure thee by Jesus Christ our God, Who was born of the Virgin, for Whose sake Thou strivest thus in this wilderness, conceal not Thy life from me, but relate all things unto me, that Thou mayest make manifest the magnificent works of God! Tell me all things for God's sake; for Thou shalt speak not for vainglory, but to edify me, a sinner and unworthy man. I believe my God, for Whom Thou livest, that for this very purpose I was guided into this wilderness, that God might make manifest Thy works; for it is not in the power of our weakness to resist the judgments of God. For if Christ our God had not willed that Thou and Thy struggle should be made known, He would neither have revealed thee unto me, nor strengthened me for so great a journey—one who was never willing or able before to go forth out of my cell."

items.english_text: And while the elder waited and wept unceasingly, she began to relate her life, speaking thus: "I, O father, was born in Egypt; and when I was twelve years of age, while my parents were still living, I cast off their affection and went away to Alexandria. And having lost my first modesty, I gave myself over unrestrainedly to a life of vanity and sin. I am ashamed even to call to mind that dishonor, yet I will speak briefly, that thou mayest know the excess of my fallen passions: for more than seventeen years I lived in public dissipation, receiving payment from no one, but living in poverty and spinning coarse flax, because I counted it my very life to wallow continually in earthly desires.

items.english_text: She therefore resumed her account: "That young man, hearing my bold words, laughed and departed; and I, casting away the distaff which I occasionally carried, ran toward the sea whither they were hastening. And seeing ten or more young men standing by the seashore while others had already boarded the vessel, I approached them with my customary boldness, saying: 'Take me also with you whithersoever ye go, for I shall not be unwelcome among you.' And speaking other idle words, I moved them all to laughter; and they took me aboard their ship, and thence we set sail.

items.english_text: "How shall I relate unto thee what followed, O father? What tongue can utter, or what ear can bear to hear the evil deeds committed by me along the way and upon the ship? Believe me, O father, I marvel how the sea endured my lawlessness! How did the earth not open its mouth and swallow me down alive into hades, who had led astray so many souls? Yet I think that God was seeking my repentance; for He desires not the death of sinners, but awaits their conversion with long-suffering.[^1387]

items.english_text: "Thus I arrived in Jerusalem, and during all the days before the feast I continued in the same evil ways, and even worse. And when the holy feast of the Exaltation of the Precious Cross arrived,[^1388] I went about as before; and seeing everyone going very early to the church, I also went and ran along with those who were running, and entered with them into the courtyard of the church. And when the hour of the holy Exaltation arrived, as the multitude was entering into the church, I tried to enter with them, but was pushed back; and supposing that this happened because of the press of the crowd, I forced my way forward with great effort until I reached the very doors of the church within which the Life-giving Tree was displayed.

items.english_text: "Yet when I stepped upon the threshold of the church doors, all the others entered in unhindered, whereas a certain divine power held me back, not permitting me to enter; and again I attempted to enter, and was thrust far back from the doors, standing alone in the vestibule. Supposing that this happened to me because of feminine weakness, I mingled again with others who were entering, pushing with my elbows and straining with all my might; yet whenever my sinful foot touched the threshold, the church received everyone else and hindered no one, while refusing to admit me, the wretched one; as if a drawn-up detachment of soldiers were barring the entrance, so did that sudden divine power hold me back, and again I found myself in the vestibule.

For the light of saving knowledge touched the eyes of my heart, showing me that the mire of my deeds barred the entrance against me.

items.english_text: "Then I began to weep and lament, and to beat my breast, pouring forth sighs from the depths of my heart. And as I stood weeping in that place, I looked up and saw above me an icon of the Most Holy Theotokos standing on the wall; and fixing my gaze upon her, I said: 'O Virgin Lady, who didst bear in the flesh God the Word! I know, yea, I know that it is neither fitting nor right for me, a defiled sinner, to look upon the venerable icon of thee, the Ever-Virgin Mary, who hast both body and soul pure and undefiled. Rightly indeed am I, a prodigal, worthy to be hated and abhorred before thy virginal purity! Yet I have heard that God, Whom thou didst bear, became man for this very purpose, that He might call sinners to repentance.[^1389] Help me who am alone and have help from nowhere! Command that the entrance of the church be opened unto me also, and forbid me not to behold the Tree upon which Christ God was crucified in the flesh, shedding His own Blood for my redemption! Command, O Sovereign Lady, that the doors be opened unto me for the holy veneration of the Cross; and be thou my sure mediatrix and surety before Him Who was born of thee, that henceforth I will never again defile this flesh; but as soon as I have beheld the Tree of the Cross of Thy Son, I will renounce this world and its deeds, and will immediately go forth whithersoever thou, as my surety, shalt guide me!'

items.english_text: "Having cried out thus, I went forth from the courtyard of the church and walked rapidly. And a certain man, seeing me walking, gave me three copper coins, saying: 'Accept these, my mother.' Taking them, I bought three loaves of bread, and asked the baker who sold me the loaves: 'Sir, which is the way to the Jordan?' Learning which city gate led in that direction, I went forth running, and walked along the road weeping. Asking my way as I went, I completed the day's journey—for it was about the third hour of the day when I beheld the Precious Cross—and toward sunset I reached the Church of St. John the Baptist, which stands near the banks of the Jordan.[^1391]

items.english_text: "Having prayed first in the church, I went down immediately to the Jordan and washed my face and hands in that holy water; and afterward I partook of the Most Pure and Life-giving Mysteries of Christ in the Church of the Forerunner. Then I ate half of one loaf, drank of the water of the Jordan, and slept that night upon the ground. Early the next morning, finding a small boat there, I crossed over to the opposite bank of the Jordan; and again I prayed to my Guide, the Theotokos, to direct me whithersoever seemed good to her.

items.english_text: Zosimas said unto the venerable one: "How many years have passed, my lady, since thou didst take up thy dwelling in this wilderness?" And she answered: "I think that forty and seven years have elapsed since I went forth from the Holy City." Zosimas said unto her: "And what dost thou find for thy nourishment, my lady?" She said: "I brought two and a half loaves of bread with me when I crossed the Jordan; and little by little they dried up and became hard as stone, and partaking of them sparingly a little at a time, I subsisted on them for several years."

items.english_text: Zosimas asked: "How then hast thou passed so many years without harm, suffering no distress from so sudden a change of life?" She answered: "Thou hast questioned me now, Abba Zosimas, concerning a matter of which I tremble even to speak; for if I call to mind all those perils which I endured, and the fierce thoughts that assailed me, I fear lest I be seized by them once again." Zosimas said unto her: "O my lady, I beseech thee, leave nothing untold that thou canst declare unto me; for since thou hast begun, relate the whole matter unto me until the end."

items.english_text: And she said unto him: "Believe me, Abba Zosimas, for seventeen years I struggled in this wilderness against my own passionate thoughts as against fierce wild beasts! For whenever I began to taste a little food, immediately there came upon me a craving for the meats and fish that were in Egypt;[^1393] and I craved also the wine which I had loved so much—for when I was in the world I drank much wine, whereas here, not having even a drop of water to taste, I burned with thirst and endured grievous distress.

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: "There came upon me also a perverse desire for worldly songs, troubling my mind and stirring me to chant the vain melodies I had learned in the world; but immediately shedding tears and beating my breast, I called to mind the vows which I had made before departing into this wilderness. In spirit I would stand before the icon of the Most Holy Theotokos, my Surety, weeping before her and imploring her to drive away from me the thoughts that tormented my wretched soul. And when I had wept long enough and beaten my breast fervently, I would behold a calm light shining round about me from every side, and a great stillness would replace the tempest.

items.section: At the Aposticha, Stichera for the Departed, Tone 8, Podoben: "O most marvelous wonder" (Ѽ пресла́внагѡ чꙋдесѐ)

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: "Whenever turbulent thoughts rose up again within my heart, I cast myself down upon the earth and watered it with tears, believing that my Surety herself stood before me, arraigning me as a transgressor and showing me the punishment due to my breach of covenant; and I would not rise from the ground night or day until that sweet light shone upon me again and scattered the thoughts that troubled me. Thus I lifted the eyes of my mind unceasingly toward my Surety, beseeching her to succor me in this desert; and truly I had her as my helper and the furtherance of my repentance.

items.english_text: "In this manner I completed seventeen years, enduring ten thousand perils; and from that time until this day my Helper hath preserved me in all things." Zosimas said unto her: "And hast thou had no need since then of food or clothing?" She answered: "After finishing those loaves of bread over the course of seventeen years, as I told thee, I was nourished by the wild herbs and roots found in this desert. As for the garment which I wore when I crossed the Jordan, it became tattered and fell away completely; and thereafter I suffered great affliction from the cold of winter and the scorching heat of summer, burning under the sun and freezing and shivering in the frost, so that many times I fell to the earth and lay motionless as if without breath.

items.english_text: "Having struggled thus against manifold afflictions and temptations, from that time until this present day the manifold power of God hath preserved my sinful soul and humble body. When I reflect only upon the great evils from which the Lord hath delivered me, I possess inexhaustible nourishment in the hope of my salvation; for I am fed and clothed by the word of God, Who upholds the universe. For man doth not live by bread alone, and because of having no shelter, those who have stripped off the garment of sin have embraced the rock!"[^1394]

items.english_text: Having spoken thus and concluded her account, she bowed down to make a prostration before the elder; and the elder cried aloud with tears: "Blessed is God, Who works great and marvelous things, glorious and unsearchable, whereof there is no number![^1395] Blessed is God, Who hath shown me how great are the gifts He bestows upon those who fear Him! Truly, O Lord, Thou dost never forsake them that seek Thee!"

items.english_text: And when the elder wished to fall at her feet, she took hold of him and permitted him not to prostrate himself, saying unto him: "Concerning all these things which thou hast heard, O father, I adjure thee by Jesus Christ our God and Savior to speak of them to no man until God shall take me from the earth. Now depart in peace, and in the coming year thou shalt see me again, preserved by the grace of God. Only do for the Lord's sake that which I now enjoin upon thee: During the Great Fast of the coming year, cross not over the Jordan as ye are accustomed to do in the monastery."

items.english_text: Zosimas marveled upon hearing that she knew even the rule of the monastery, and could say nothing else save only: "Glory be to God, Who bestows great gifts upon them that love Him!" And she continued: "Remain, therefore, in the monastery, Abba, as I tell thee; for even if thou shouldst attempt to go forth before the time, it will not be possible for thee. And on the evening of Holy and Great Thursday, which commemorates the Mystical Supper of Christ,[^1396] place in a sacred vessel worthy of such a mystery a portion of the Life-giving Body and Blood of Christ our God, and bring it for me; and wait for me on the bank of the Jordan that lies near the inhabited world, so that I may come and partake of the Life-giving Gifts. For since the time when I communicated in the Church of the Forerunner before crossing the Jordan, until this day I have not received that sanctification; therefore I thirst for it with unrestrainable longing, and I implore thee not to disdain my request, but certainly to bring me the Divine and Life-giving Mysteries at the very hour when the Lord made His disciples partakers of the Divine Supper. And as for John, the abbot of the monastery in which thou dwellest, say unto him: 'Look to thyself and to thy flock,[^1397] for there are certain things there that require correction.' Yet I wish thee not to say this unto him now, but when the Lord shall permit thee."

And Zosimas, falling upon his knees and kissing the ground whereon her feet had stood, gave glory and thanks unto God; and he returned through the wilderness rejoicing and praising Christ our God, arriving back at the monastery on the appointed day when the other brethren also returned.

items.english_text: Throughout that entire year the elder kept silence, daring to tell no one anything of what he had seen, while praying earnestly within himself that God would show him again that desired countenance; and he grieved and counted the length of the year heavy to bear, wishing that the whole year might pass like a single day if that were possible.

items.english_text: When the First Sunday of the Holy and Great Fast arrived, the other brethren went forth chanting according to the custom and order of the monastery; Zosimas, however, was seized by a feverish illness and was compelled to remain behind in the monastery. Then Zosimas remembered the words spoken by the venerable one: "Even if thou shouldst wish to go forth from the monastery, it will not be possible for thee." After Not many days he was healed of his infirmity and remained within the monastery.

items.english_text: Though the saint delayed, Zosimas did not allow himself to slumber, but gazed intently toward the desert, longing to behold her whom he earnestly desired. And sitting on the bank, the elder conversed within himself, saying: "What if my unworthiness hath hindered her from coming? What if she came already, and not finding me, turned back?" Speaking thus, he sighed and wept; and lifting his eyes to heaven, he prayed to God, saying: "Deprive me not, O Sovereign Master, of beholding again that face which Thou didst grant me to see, lest I depart empty, bearing the burden of my sins for my own reproof!"

For there is no boat here; how then shall she cross the Jordan to come unto me, an unworthy man? Woe to my unworthiness! Woe is me, who hath deprived me of such a blessing?"

items.english_text: While the elder was pondering these things, behold, the holy woman arrived and stood on the opposite bank of the river, coming out of the desert. Zosimas rose up rejoicing with joy and glorifying God, though still wrestling in his mind with the thought that she would not be able to cross the Jordan. Looking across, he saw her sign the waters of the Jordan with the sign of the Precious Cross—for the night, as he said, was bright with the full moon—and simultaneously with making the sign of the Cross, she stepped down upon the water and walked across the surface of the river toward him!

items.english_text: When the elder attempted to make a prostration before her, she forbade him while still walking upon the water, crying aloud: "What dost thou, Abba, seeing that thou art a priest and art carrying the Divine Mysteries?" Stepping off the water onto the bank, she said to the elder: "Bless, father, bless!" He answered her with trembling—for amazement had seized him at that transcendent miracle—saying: "Truly God is not false in promising that those who purify themselves shall become like unto God so far as is possible![^1398] Glory be to Thee, O Christ our God, Who hast shown me through this Thy handmaid how far distant I stand from the measure of perfection!"

items.english_text: When he had spoken thus, she asked him to recite the sacred Symbol of Faith ("I believe in one God") and the Lord's Prayer ("Our Father Who art in the heavens"). When the prayer was concluded, she partook of the Undefiled Mysteries of Christ, and according to the custom gave the kiss of peace to the elder; then raising her hands toward heaven, she sighed and wept, crying aloud: "Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace, according to Thy word; for mine eyes have seen Thy salvation, which Thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples!"[^1399]

items.english_text: And she said again to the elder: "Pardon me, Abba Zosimas, and fulfill one more desire of mine: return now to thy monastery, guarded by the peace of God; and in the coming year come again to that same dry torrent bed where I first conversed with thee. Come, I pray thee for the Lord's sake, and Thou shalt see me again according as the Lord wills." He answered her: "Would that it were possible for me to follow behind thee from this hour and gaze continually upon thy venerable countenance! Yet grant this one entreaty of an old man, and taste a little of the food which I have brought for thee." And saying this, he showed her the basket which he carried.

And she said again to the elder: "Pray to the Lord for me, O father, pray for me, and remember always my wretchedness!"

items.english_text: He bowed down at her feet, asking her to pray to God for the Church, the emperors, and himself; and having asked this with tears, he let her depart, groaning and lamenting, for he did not dare to detain any longer one who could not be held back even if he wished. Signing the Jordan once more with the sign of the Cross, she walked back across the waters as she had done before. And the elder returned to his monastery filled with great joy and holy fear, reproaching himself only because he had neglected to learn the name of the saint, though hoping to learn it in the following year.

items.english_text: When another year had passed, Zosimas went forth again into the wilderness according to custom, hastening toward that marvelous sight. Walking through the desert and noticing certain signs of the place he sought, he looked to the right and to the left like a keen hunter seeking to capture a most sweet quarry. When he saw no movement anywhere, he began to weep; and lifting his eyes to heaven, he prayed, saying: "Show me, O Lord, the unplundered treasure which Thou hast hidden in this wilderness! Show me, I beseech Thee, the angel in the flesh, of whom the whole world is not worthy!"[^1400]

Running to her, he washed the feet of the blessed one with his tears, not daring to touch any other part of her body.

items.english_text: Having wept for a long time and chanted psalms suited to the occasion, he offered the funeral prayers and said within himself: "Ought I to bury the relic of the holy one, or might this perhaps be displeasing to her?" As he said this, he noticed beside her head an inscription traced upon the ground in these words: "Bury, Abba Zosimas, in this place the body of humble Mary; render dust unto dust, and pray to the Lord for me, who departed in the month of Pharmouthi according to the Egyptians, which is April according to the Romans, on the first day of the month, on the very night of the saving Passion of Christ, after partaking of the Divine and Mystical Supper."[^1401]

items.english_text: Reading this inscription, the elder wondered at first who could have written it, since she had told him that she had never learned letters; yet he rejoiced exceedingly to learn the name of the saint, and understood clearly that immediately after partaking of the Divine Mysteries at the Jordan, she had been transported in a single hour to this place—a journey that had taken him twenty days of wearisome travel—and had departed immediately unto God.

items.english_text: Glorifying God, and wetting the earth and the relic of the saint with his tears, the elder said within himself: "It is time now, poor Zosimas, to fulfill what is commanded; yet how shalt thou dig, wretched man, having no tool in thy hands?" Saying this, he saw a small piece of wood lying nearby on the ground; picking it up, he began to dig with it. The ground, however, was parched and hard, and yielded not at all to the elder's efforts as he labored and sweated without accomplishing anything.

items.english_text: Sighing deeply from the bottom of his heart, he looked up and saw a great lion standing beside the relic of the blessed Mary and licking the soles of her feet. At the sight of the wild beast the elder trembled with fear, especially remembering how the holy one had told him that she had never seen a wild beast; but signing himself with the sign of the Cross, he trusted that he would be kept unharmed by the power of the one lying before him. And the lion began to fawn gently upon the elder, greeting him with mild movements as if saluting him.

items.english_text: Zosimas then said to the lion: "O great beast, since this holy one hath commanded me to bury her body, and I am an old man unable to dig—having no mattock with me, and being too far away to return and fetch one—do thou therefore perform the work with thy claws, that we may commit to the earth the all-holy tabernacle of the saint!" Immediately upon hearing these words, the lion dug out with its front paws a trench deep enough to cover the body of her who was being buried.

items.english_text: Having washed the feet of the saint once more with his tears, and entreated her earnestly to pray on behalf of all, the elder covered her body with earth in the presence of the lion, her body being clad solely in the tattered cloak which Zosimas had cast to her at their first meeting. Then both departed: the lion withdrew into the inner wilderness as gently as a lamb, while Zosimas returned to his monastery blessing and praising Christ our God.

items.english_text: Upon reaching the monastery, the elder related to all the monks everything that he had seen and heard from her, concealing nothing from them; and all marveled upon hearing of the magnificent works of God, celebrating with fear and faith and love the commemoration of the saint. And Abbot John found certain matters in the monastery requiring correction, just as the holy one had foretold, and set them right with the help of God. Zosimas himself reposed in that same monastery after reaching nearly a hundred years of age.

Whether others also have written the life of the saint with fuller knowledge of her deeds has not come to my awareness; yet to the best of my ability I have recorded this account, placing nothing above the truth.

items.english_text: And may God, Who works great miracles and bestows great gifts upon those who take refuge in Him in faith, grant a reward unto those who read and listen to this account, and to the one who arranged for this narrative to be committed to writing; and may He count them worthy of the blessed portion of this saint, Mary, concerning whom this narrative is told, together with all who have pleased Him from the beginning by contemplative vision and virtuous deeds! Let us also give glory unto God the eternal King, that He may grant us to find mercy in the Day of Judgment in Christ Jesus our Lord, to Whom belongs all glory, honor, dominion, and worship, together with the unoriginate Father and the All-Holy, Good, and Life-giving Spirit, now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

items.english_text: *Compiled from an ancient writing, setting forth a glorious remembrance of the miracle which took place when the Persians and Barbarians besieged the Imperial City with warfare, and perished by the judgment of God after being put to the test, whereas the City was preserved unharmed through the prayers of our Most Pure Lady the Theotokos; from which time this service of thanksgiving has been chanted, calling that day the Akathist.*[^1402]

items.english_text: In the days of Heraclius, the Emperor of the Greeks, Khosrow, who held the sovereignty of the Persians, sent his general Shahrbaraz with a great multitude of troops against the entire eastern region under Greek rule, sweeping across it like fiery lightning, burning, scorching, and destroying all things.[^1403] Having laid waste the eastern lands with great boldness and mocked the Greeks whom he encountered there—for there was no one able to resist him or cut short his mighty invasion, the Greek forces having been previously humbled and exhausted by the harsh and ferocious tyranny of the soldier Phocas, who had ruled the empire like a tyrant rather than an emperor—Shahrbaraz advanced as far as Chalcedon; and pitching his camp round about it, he prepared everything for the destruction of the Great and Imperial City, devising and counseling every stratagem toward that end.

items.english_text: Seeing these things, Emperor Heraclius, who had newly assumed the throne after the tyrant Phocas and was weighed down by great affliction and toil, left the capital and sailed across the Euxine Sea—that is, the Black Sea—having gathered whatever military forces remained, and suddenly, without anyone knowing of his movement, marched into the lands of Persia. Learning of the Emperor's departure, the Khagan of the Scythians immediately seized his opportunity: he filled the sea with vessels hollowed out of single logs (which for this reason are called *monoxyla* in the Greek tongue),[^1404] and covered the dry land with horsemen and foot soldiers.

items.english_text: Meanwhile, the people remaining within the Imperial City were comforted and instructed by Sergius, who was then Patriarch, not to lose hope: "Take courage, my children," said the Patriarch, "and let us place the hope of our salvation in God, lifting up our hands and our eyes unto Him with all our soul! He will deliver us from the evils that encompass us, and will scatter all the barbarian counsels devised against us." Strengthened by these words of the Patriarch, the inhabitants of the city persevered in faith toward the Most Pure Theotokos and toward Christ our God, Who for His love of mankind was well-pleased to become incarnate of her; and awaiting His mercy upon themselves, they endured in hope—which shortly thereafter they were counted worthy to receive, not falling short of their expectation.

items.english_text: Now Patrician Bonos, who had been left behind by the Emperor to guard the city, spared no effort in devising every defense possible against the enemy; "For God wills," said he, "that we should not sit idle and inactive, but should labor and take forethought on our own part while placing all our hope of salvation in Him; for thus did Joshua the son of Nun command ambushes and stratagems to be prepared against the men of Ai, and thus did Gideon arm his men with water pitchers and torches against Midian."[^1405] Patrician Bonos therefore fortified the walls of the city and prepared everything needed for defense; while Patriarch Sergius, taking up the sacred icons of the Mother of God—especially that upon which the Infant Savior is depicted borne in His Mother's arms—walked in procession around the walls of the city, establishing thereby a firm bulwark for the citizens, and bringing terror, flight, and ruin upon the opposing barbarians—

items.english_text: Before three days had passed after the conflagration, the entire host of the Scythian commander advanced against the city; and so vast was the multitude of the adversaries, arrayed in numberless ranks and fortified in full armor, that to speak truly there were ten Scythians gathered against every single Greek! Yet our Champion Leader, the Most Pure Sovereign Lady who fights on behalf of Christians and is a speedy helper to those who call upon her, came to the aid of a detachment of soldiers at her divine Church called the *Pege* (the Life-giving Spring),[^1407] where they slew a great number of the attacking Scythians. This manifest assistance granted to the Christians by the all-powerful Commander, the Mother of God, not only cast down the enemy before the Greeks, but also reduced the boastful arrogance of the Scythian warlord to bewilderment through such generalship on the part of the Mother of God, foreshadowing the complete destruction that was shortly to overtake them.

items.english_text: Beholding so great a fall of the enemy before the citizens, and recognizing it as a sign and beginning of the foes' ruin, the Greeks took heart and were filled with great courage; and day by day they stood ready to join battle against them, having the Mother of God fighting alongside them, rendering them stronger and frustrating the stratagems, strength, and assaults of the Scythians.

items.english_text: After these things, by the common consent of the Patriarch, the Prefect Bonos, and the people, envoys were sent forth from the city bearing gifts to speak words of peace to the Scythians and invite them to a truce. The Khagan, however, being beast-like in temper rather than human, and exceedingly covetous in character, accepted the gifts while spurning the proposals of peace, and sent the envoys back empty-handed, saying only this unto them: "Deceive not yourselves concerning the God in Whom ye trust! Assuredly tomorrow I will seize your city with my hand like a bird in a nest, and will lay it waste; and out of my own clemency I will let you all go free wearing only a single garment apiece! Depart then from the city whithersoever ye wish, for I shall show you no greater humanity than this"—after that wretched man had first uttered many blasphemies against Christ our God and against Her who bore Him.

items.english_text: Hearing these words from the returning envoys, the inhabitants of the city—all the priests, the clergy, the monastics, and the entire populace—groaned from the depths of their hearts; and hastening to the holy churches of God, they lifted up their hands toward heaven and prayed with abundant tears, saying: "O Lord our Defender, O Lord, look down from Thy holy dwelling-place and behold this foul barbarian and those with him, who have dared to blaspheme Thy holy and great Name! Cast him down, O Lord our Protector, lest it be said among the nations: 'Where is their God?'[^1408] For Thou art our God, Who resistest the proud and lookest upon the humble! Thy dominion is incomparable and Thy Kingdom indestructible; hear the words which this barbarian hath sent to reproach Thee, Who reignest over all! Deliver the city of Thine inheritance and the people called by Thy Name!"

items.english_text: Thus did the weeping people pray; and God prevented the Persians from crossing over to join the Khagan as they had agreed, slaying no small number of the envoys whom they sent back and forth to one another. Fighting along the outskirts for two and three days and assaulting various sectors without rest, both enemy hosts prepared a simultaneous general assault according to their pact: by land they brought up siege engines to batter down the walls of the city, while by sea they armed the countless Scythian *monoxyla*, intending at one and the same day and hour to strike the Imperial City simultaneously by land and by sea.

items.english_text: Yet who can recount the miracles of God wrought at that hour, or who can declare the tender compassion of the Virgin toward us? For when the Khagan filled the bay of the Golden Horn with *monoxyla* and armed warriors therein—attempting by land to overthrow the walls while by sea the forces in the Golden Horn stood ready to scale the city—our Lord and God, Whom they had blasphemed and Who is God over all, through the prayers of the Virgin Theotokos who bore Him, showed their hopes to be vain and fruitless! On every side of the land walls the Greek soldiers slew so vast a multitude of the enemy that the survivors were no longer able even to burn their dead.

items.english_text: Such was the fate of those who fought by land and strove to cast down the walls. As for the *monoxyla* together with all the warriors aboard them, opposite the divine Church of our Sovereign Lady the Theotokos at Blachernae, she sank them all suddenly in a single moment by raising a dreadful and violent tempest! For as soon as those vessels drew near her divine Church, the sea rose up exceedingly high and divided at the divine command, engulfing and sinking them all immediately together with the *monoxyla* themselves.

items.slavonic_text: двигшым, ско́рw потопи́вши, дѣ́ло морски́ми струя́ми сотворѝ: на ню́же єди́нꙋ спасе́нїа наде́ждꙋ возложи́вше, и жре́бїй єя̀ ѿ напа́дшихъ лю́тыхъ безстра́стенъ вкꙋ́пѣ сохрани́вши. Тогда́ бо и са́мъ старѣ́йшина и́хъ хага́нъ, самови́децъ бы́въ свои́хъ во́й поги́бели, та́мw нѣ́гдѣ со хра́брыми свои́ми ко́нники, на высо́цѣ мѣ́стѣ стоя̀, рꙋка́ма по лицꙋ̀ и по пе́рсемъ бїя́шеся. Сꙋ́щїи же внꙋ́трь гра́да, проти́вꙋ врагѡ́мъ бра́нь твора́ще, поне́же ꙋви́дѣша въ мо́ри бы́вшꙋю врагѡ́мъ поги́бель, а́бїе бж҃е́ственною си́лою возмо́гше, и Дв҃ы Бц҃ы крѣ́постїю ѡгра́ждшеся, врата̀ гра́да ѿве́рзше, крича́ще и восклица́юще, на врагѝ итека́хꙋ. Толи́ка ꙋ́бw ра́дость и си́ла ѡбдержа́ше гра́дскїѧ вẃи, ва́рвары же боѧ́знь велїа. И бѣ̀ ви́дѣти пресла́вно воево́дство Влчцы на́шеѧ Бц҃ы, ꙗ́кw и ма́лїи ѻ́троцы, и жєны̀ ꙋстреми́шася на ва́рвары, и къ са́мымъ вїи вра̑гъ свои́хъ вхожда́хꙋ: и толи́ко ꙋбїйство ва́рварѡмъ сотвори́ша, єли́ко невозможно сло́вомъ исчестѝ. Та́мw вои́стиннꙋ соверши́ся рече́нное, єди́нъ гона́ше ты́сящꙋ, а два̀ тмꙋ̀. Та́ковꙋ пречи́стая и Дв҃а Бц҃а и Влчца крѣ́пость некрѣ́пкимъ, и си́лꙋ немощны́мъ дарова̀. Ꙗ́коже со́лнцꙋ заше́дшꙋ, и но́щи наста́вши, бра́нныѧ сосꙋ́ды, ꙗ́же бяхꙋ на коле́сѣхъ привезѡ́ша ва́рвари, на вза́тїе гра́да, вся̀ ѻгню̀ преда́ша: и свои́хъ трꙋдѡ́въ и ко́зней дѣ́лателемъ самѣ̑мъ запали́телемъ бы́ти, бл҃года́ть Бц҃ѣ ꙋꙋтро́ннейшей и́мъ. Стѣ́лъ же и вся̀ гражда́не рꙋ́ки на нб҃о воздѣ́вше, со слеза́ми бл҃годарє́нїе пода́хꙋ, и глаго́лахꙋ: десни́ца твоѧ̀ Гдⷭ҇и, просла́вися въ крѣ́пости, десна́ѧ твоѧ̀ рꙋка̀ Гдⷭ҇и, сокрꙋшѝ врагѝ, и мно́жествомъ сла́вы твоеѧ̀ сте́рлъ єсѝ сопоста́ты. И та́кw ꙋ́бw безу́мный хага́нъ, со мно́жествомъ безчисле́нныхъ вẃй прише́дъ, со сра́момъ возврати́ся. Та́коже и пе́рсскїй вẃи приведїй воево́да, рꙋкꙋ на ꙋстѣ́хъ положи́въ, и лицѐ закры́въ, ꙗ́кw ѿ толи́кихъ ты́сящъ ма́лое число̀ съ собо́ю ꙋведѐ, съ сра́момъ ко свое́й странѣ̀ дости́же. Та́кw бж҃е́ственнагw смотре́нїа и бл҃гости служи́тельница, пречи́стая и пренепоро́чная Бц҃а, хрⷭ҇тїа́нская держа́вная помо́щница, є́же ѡ на́шемъ застꙋпле́нїи крѣ́пость показа̀, таково̀ вели́кое на́мъ и пресла́вное спасе́нїе дарова̀. Тѣ́мже, на воспомина́нїа такова́гw бл҃годѣя́нїа, ны́нѣшнїй моле́бный вселю́дскїй собо́ръ твори́мъ, и всено́щный содѣва́емъ пра́здникъ, бл҃года́рственныѧ пѣ̑сни принося́ще, и́же и Несѣда́льно вселе́нскаѧ Цр҃ковь прире́кши пра́здникъ се́й, Мт҃и Бж҃їей пра́здновати, ко вре́ма сїѐ, єгда̀ и побѣ́да Бж҃їею Мт҃рїю бы́сть, А́ка́ѳїсто наре́кши, си́рѣчь, Несѣда́льно. Поне́же та́кw сотвори́ша цр҃ко́вницы тогда̀, и лю́дїе гра́да всѝ.
items.english_text: Now those within the city, waging battle against the enemies, when they beheld the destruction that had befallen the foes in the sea, immediately waxing strong by divine power and fortified by the might of the Virgin Theotokos, opened the gates of the city, and shouting and crying aloud, rushed upon the enemies. Such great joy and strength possessed the city's warriors, while great fear seized the barbarians. And it was a marvelous sight to behold the glorious generalship of our Sovereign Lady the Theotokos: for even young youths and women rushed upon the barbarians and attacked the very necks of their enemies; and they wrought such slaughter among the barbarians as is impossible to recount in words. There truly was fulfilled that which was spoken: one chased a thousand, and two put ten thousands to flight. Such strength did the Most Pure Virgin Theotokos and Sovereign Lady grant unto the weak, and such power unto the infirm.

items.slavonic_text: По прехожде́нїи же три́десѧти и шестѝ лѣ́тъ, при цр҃твѣ̀ Кwнстанти́на брада́тагw, па́ки дости́же срацы́нскїй Роїстоло́мъ вели́кїй со мно́жествомъ корабле́й на цр҃твꙋющїй то́й гра́дъ. И а́бїе при́ста́ша при брѣ́зѣ ко ꙋдо́мꙋ, ѿ ни́хже бра́ни по мо́рю по вся̀ днѝ на гра́дъ быва́хꙋ, ѿ ве́шнагw вре́мене и до ѻ́сени, зимова́ти же ѿхожда́хꙋ въ Ку́зїкъ. И па́ки къ веснѣ̀ прихода́ще къ царю̀ гра́дꙋ, и па́ки ѿ мо́рѧ бра́нь твора́хꙋ: и за се́дмь лѣ́тъ крѣ́пкw ра́товахꙋ. Мно́гїа же кораблѝ своѧ̀ погуби́ша, и съ сосꙋ́дженными вẃи, и вся̀ ꙗ́же принеслѝ бяхꙋ съ собо́ю ꙋстрое́нїа на потре́бꙋ, и возврати́шася и ті́и съ вели́кою тщето́ю ко своѧ̀ си. И во страна́хъ салїйскихъ бы́вше, лю́тымъ и проти́внымъ вѣ́трѡмъ дохнꙋ́вшымъ на ня̀, пра́веднымъ гнѣ́вомъ Бж҃їимъ погибо́ша, предста́тельствомъ Бж҃їѧ Мт҃ре въ мо́ри всѝ потопи́шася. Та́коже и на разли́чнаѧ времена̀ томꙋ̀ Бг҃охрани́момꙋ гра́дꙋ прирази́вшеся ѡкая́ннїи, неи́стовное и́хъ стремле́нїе исполня́юще, бездѣ́льны и стꙋда̀ испо́лнены возвраща́хꙋся.
items.english_text: The Prefect and all the citizens, lifting up their hands unto heaven, offered thanksgiving with tears, saying: "Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, hath broken the enemies, and in the multitude of Thy glory Thou hast crushed the adversaries!"[^1410] And thus the foolish Khagan, having arrived with a multitude of countless troops, returned in shame. In like manner also the general who had led the Persian troops, laying his hand upon his mouth and covering his face, because out of so many thousands he led away only a small number with himself, reached his own country in disgrace.

items.english_text: Thus the servant of divine providence and goodness, the Most Pure and Undefiled Theotokos, the sovereign helper of Christians, showed her strength in our defense and granted us so great and glorious a salvation. Therefore, in remembrance of such a benefaction, we assemble this present solemn congregational gathering of all the people, and we celebrate an all-night feast, offering songs of thanksgiving. The Universal Church hath named this feast the "Unseated Hymn" (*Akathistos*), to be celebrated in honor of the Mother of God at this season when the victory was wrought by the Mother of God, calling it *Akathistos*, that is, *Unseated*; because thus did the clergy and all the people of the city perform it at that time.[^1411]

items.english_text: After the passing of thirty-six years, in the reign of Constantine the Bearded, the great Saracen fleet (*Rhodostolos*) arrived once again with a multitude of ships against that imperial city.[^1412] And they anchored immediately along the shore at the inlet, from which they waged warfare by sea against the city daily, from the springtime until the autumn, departing to spend the winter in Cyzicus. And returning again in the spring to the imperial city, they again waged warfare from the sea, contending fiercely for seven years.

items.slavonic_text: по стѣ́намъ гра́да, воздви́гше къ Бг҃ꙋ рꙋ́цѣ, и глаго́лахꙋ: Воскрⷭ҇нѝ Гдⷭ҇и, помозѝ на́мъ, и не ѿри́ни люде́й твои́хъ до конца̀: ꙗ́кw сѐ вразѝ твоѝ козни́шася, и ненави́дящїи тебѐ воздвиго́ша главꙋ̀. Не да́ждь достоѧ́нїа твоегѡ̀ въ поноше́нїе, є́же ѡблада́ти над̾ на́ми ꙗ́зыкѡмъ, да не когда̀ рекꙋ́тъ: гдѣ̀ є́сть Бг҃ъ и́хъ; но да позна́ютъ, ꙗ́кw и́ма тебѐ Гдⷭ҇ь Іи҃съ Хрⷭ҇то́съ, въ сла́вꙋ Бг҃а Ѻц҃а̀. Єди́нъ же нѣ́кто ѿ проти́вныхъ сраци́нъ конни́къ, хва́льнымъ гласы Кwнстанти́нъ гра́дъ именꙋѧ, и це́рковь просты́мъ и́менемъ, Софїю нарица́ѧ, въ нѣ́кое ро́вище и съ коне́мъ до́лꙋ па́дя и́здыше. Но и проповѣ́дникъ и́хъ, на высо́кое дре́во взлѣ́зъ, да пропо́вѣстъ скве́рнꙋю и́хъ моли́твꙋ, и то́й та́коже па́дъ до́лꙋ, ѡкаѧ́ннw безбо́жнꙋю свою̀ дꙋ́шꙋ изве́рже. Поте́мъ и на Бо́лгары воева́ти совѣща́ша: два̀ бо бѣ́ста воево́ды, и єди́нъ ꙋ́бw ѡста̀ разори́ти цр҃твꙋющїй гра́дъ, другїй же и́йде на Бо́лгары воева́ти. Съ ни́миже ра́товався, побѣжде́нъ бы́сть ѿ ни́хъ: и падо́ша ѿ вẃй єгѡ̀ мно́жае двою̀ тмꙋ̀, ѡста́вшїи же со сра́момъ возврати́шася къ свои̑мъ. Покуша́хꙋся же по ѡбраще́нїи ѿ Бѡ́лгаръ, приведе́ными корабля̀, на влахе́рнскꙋю странꙋ̀ прїитѝ. Протяже́нїе же вери́гъ желѣ́зныхъ, ѿ цара̀ гра́да до Гала́ты, возбрани́шася, не могꙋ́ще сотвори́ти, є́же бяхꙋ совѣща́ша. Ѡплы́вше же до мѣ́ста нарица́емагw Сосѳе́нъ, и въ дрꙋги́хъ ма́лыхъ приста́нищахъ: ѿ ни́хже множа́йшїи зимо́ю лю́тою, и вѣ́тры стра́шными, разсѣ́дшеся сокрꙋши́шася: и́ныхъ же мно́жество вели́кихъ корабле́й Гре́цы сожго́ша. Гра́дъ же въ тѣснотѣ̀ бя́ше, человѣ́ческихъ потре́бъ скꙋдото́ю. Проти́внїи же вся̀ приключа́ющася и́мъ неща́днw ꙗда́хоша, и въ го́рькꙋю нꙋ́ждꙋ ѿ гла́да впа́дше, ꙗ́коже и пло́тей человѣ́ческихъ, и живо́тныхъ ме́ртвыхъ вкꙋша́ти, и ка́лъ человѣ́ческъ смѣша́юще ꙗда́хꙋ. И таковы́ѧ ра́ди нꙋ́ждныя бѣды̀, мно́гимъ имени́тымъ ѿ ни́хъ и хра́брымъ, ко гра́дꙋ прибѣ́гше приложи́тися. Ꙗ́кw ꙋ́бw дре́вле єгѵ́птяны гоня́щихъ І́и҃ла, погрузѝ во глубинѣ̀ ꙗ́кw и ка́мень, и наведѐ на ня̀ во́дꙋ морскꙋ́ю, та́коже и срацы́нѡмъ наведѐ Гдⷭ҇ь, бѣжа́щымъ ѿ цр҃твꙋющагw гра́да: те́мнымъ бо вѣ́тромъ и бꙋ́рею стра́шною и горѧ́щею мо́ре возбꙋри́вся, ѻ́ны тыся́щныѧ кораблѝ погубѝ. И́бо на Єге́йстѣй пꙋчи́нѣ множа́йшымъ корабле́мъ пловꙋ́щымъ, гра́дъ съ нб҃ѐ спадѐ вско́рѣ. Ꙗ́коже желѣ́зо ѻгню̀ прибли́жився, возкипа́етъ стꙋ́денъ, та́кожде и градо́вое ка́менїе, въ морскꙋ́ю во́дꙋ па́дшее вско́рѣ воскипѣ́ти сїю̀ сотворѝ. И таковы́мъ возкипѣ́нїемъ смолꙋ̀ корабле́й сопроти́вныхъ разварѝ, и во глубинѣ̀ всѝ погрузо́ша, трїе́мъ то́кмw на возвѣще́нїе ѡста́вшымъ. И бѣ́ше ви́дѣти на всѣ́хъ ѻстровѣ́хъ, на бре́зѣхъ же и въ приста́нищахъ, и въ зато́цѣхъ, грома́ды ме́ртвыхъ изве́ржены лежа́щыѧ. Сице́ваѧ ꙋ́бw вся̀ родо́мъ ины̑мъ, фало́мски рещѝ, да повѣ́датся, и вся́ка ꙋста̀ Хрⷭ҇тїа́нская да приглася́тъ сло́во сщ҃е́нное, съ Дв҃домъ глаго́люще: Ты̀ Гдⷭ҇и сокрꙋши́лъ єсѝ главы̑ смїе́въ въ водѣ̀. Да приложи́тся же, ꙗ́же во исхо́дѣ І́и҃левѣ пѣ́снь велегла́снw: Пои́мъ Гдⷭ҇ви, сла́внw бо просла́вися. До здѣ̀ сло́весѣ доше́дъ, и къ высотѣ̀ взира́я превели́кихъ чꙋде́съ Бг҃а и Влчⷭ҇ки, и пречи́стыя Бц҃ы еди́ныя, безгла́сенъ ѿ ꙋ́жасти быва́ю, и не ѡбрѣта́ю слове́съ подо́бныхъ дѣ́ятелемъ. Кото́рый бо велегла́сный ꙗзы́къ Дв҃ꙋ Бц҃ꙋ досто́йнw похвали́тъ; илѝ ка́кw пресла́внw воспое́тъ пресла́внꙋю єя̀ бл҃года́ть, исто́чникъ человѣколю́бїа просла́вити, и бл҃годарє́нїе принести́; Подоба́ше бо на́мъ дѣ́лы бл҃годарє́нїа принестѝ Бж҃їей Мт҃ри: таковы́ми бо весели́тся па́че, та́же сама̀, и тоя̀ Сн҃ъ, па́че свирѣ́лей, и ѻрга́нѡвъ, и мꙋсїки́йскихъ пѣ́сней. Се́ же є́сть, ꙗ́коже и А́пⷭ҇лъ речѐ: любы̀ нелицемѣ́рная, зако́на и проро́кѡвъ сꙋ́щи глава̀, братолю́бїе непрело́жное, милосе́рдїе неѡбра́тное, дѣ́вство бж҃е́ственно, бра́къ зако́ненъ, цѣломꙋ́дрїе недо́вѣдомо, пра́вда соче́танна, мꙋ́жество на стра́сти зако́нно, смы́слъ бг҃очи́ненъ, ми́лость неѡби́дна, воздержа́нїе безъ го́рдости, смире́нїе бл҃гоꙋмиле́нно: къ си̑мъ же житїѐ непоро́чно, нра́въ пра́въ, ѻбы́чай смире́нъ, ꙋ́мъ бл҃гора́зꙋменъ, ꙋста̀ бг҃оглаго́лива, ꙗзы́къ бг҃охва́ленъ, ѻ́ко нелюбодѣ́янно, рꙋ́цѣ негра́бежливѣ, но́зѣ не бы̑стрѣ на зло̀, ꙗ́рость небезслове́сна, и привлача́ющи по́мыслы неи́стовства стрѣла́ми: и ина́я, и́миже по ѻ́бразꙋ Бж҃їю созда́нъ человѣ́къ, и съ Бг҃омъ сочета́нъ, ꙗ́коже ꙋ́тварїю многоцѣ́нною и кра́сною ꙋкраша́ется. Сицевы́ми подоба́етъ Бг҃ꙋ бл҃годари́ти: поне́же бл҃годарє́нїе дѣ́лы, а не словесы̀ соста́вити, реко́ша та́кw мꙋ́дрїи. Но поне́же єстества̀ на́шегw не́мощь, и замедлѣ́нїе по́мысла, лѣни́вы на́съ твори́тъ на добродѣ́тельное потрꙋжде́нїе, и пома́лꙋ сея̀ прикаса́емся, ꙗ́коже бы рещѝ, кра́емъ перста̀. Сегѡ̀ ра́ди на предложе́нїе до́лжнагw бл҃годарє́нїа недоста́токъ и́мамы, да понѐ словесы̀ пѣ́сни принесе́мъ. Возне́сше ꙋ́бw гла́сы своя̀, и смы́слъ возвы́сивше, си́це рце́мъ со восклица́нїемъ: Ты̀ ꙋ́бw, Ѽ Влчⷭ҇це Бц҃е! человѣколю́бїе єстество́мъ имꙋ́щи, не ѡста́вила єсѝ ро́да на́шегw хрⷭ҇тїа́нскагw застꙋпа́ющи, ꙗ́коже Мт҃и чадолюби́ва кꙋ́пнw и ми́лостива. Та́кw при́снw твоѧ̑ бл҃годѣя́нїа да́рꙋеши на́мъ, спаса́ющи и покрыва́ющи, и сохраня́ющи, ѿ бѣ́дъ свобожда́ющи, и ѿ напа́стей премѣня́ющи. Мы́ же си́хъ ра́ди бл҃годари́мъ, и проповѣ́даемъ бл҃года́ть, не таи́мъ бл҃годѣя́нїа, пое́мъ велегла́снw твоѧ̑ чꙋдеса̀, по́мощь прославля́емъ, промышле́нїе велича́емъ, застꙋпле́нїе воспѣва́емъ, помо́щницꙋ тя̀ бл҃готво́рнꙋ и́мамы: милосе́рдїе твоѐ славосло́вимъ, и ѡ мнѡ́гихъ ꙋ́бw воспомина́юще твоѧ̑ вели́каѧ дарова́нїа, и ѿ коли́кихъ бѣ́дъ изба́вихомся тобо́ю. Сїя̑ тебѣ̀ бл҃года́рственныя пѣ̑сни ꙗ́кw до́лгъ прино́симъ, не ꙗ́кw досто́йны сꙋ́ща твоему̀ бл҃годѣя́нїю: ѻба́че ꙋ́лыбей дѣте́й нѣмова́нїе, ѡ настоя́щихъ же и ѡскорбля́ющихъ на́съ, мо́лимъ твою̀ бы́стрꙋю по́мощь, тре́бꙋемъ твоегѡ̀ застꙋпле́нїя, разрѣшѝ сꙋ́щыя посредѣ̀ на́съ претыка̑нїя. Разженѝ ѡблежа́щїй ны̀ ѻ́блакъ и тмꙋ̀, и́миже ꙗ́кw и въ нощнѣ́й бра́ни ꙋязвля́еми быва́емъ, па́че же рещѝ, ꙗ́кw неи́стови, свои́хъ пло́тей снѣда́емся, не разꙋмѣ́юще сро́дства, и єдиноплеме́нства не помышля́юще, и такова́я твори́ти дерза́емъ нѣ́цыи, и́же тогѡ́же Дх҃а, єди́нагw Хрⷭ҇та̀, тоя́же вѣ́ры, тогѡ́же креще́нїя, и єди́ныя Цр҃кве, и тѣ́хже Та́инъ сподо́блени бы́вше.
items.english_text: They lost many of their ships, together with the soldiers stationed aboard them and all the equipment which they had brought with them for their need; and they also returned with great loss unto their own lands. And when they were in the regions of Syllaeum, fierce and contrary winds blew upon them, and by the righteous wrath of God they perished, all being drowned in the sea through the intercession of the Mother of God. In like manner, at diverse times the wretched ones, throwing themselves against that God-guarded city to fulfill their furious impulse, returned empty-handed and filled with shame.

items.slavonic_text: Но да сло́ва не простира́емъ да́лѣ. Сегѡ̀ ра́ди мо́лимся, всест҃а́я Влчⷭ҇це, твоемꙋ̀ бл҃госе́рдїю, щедро́ты твоя̑ прїѧ́ти лю́демъ твои̑мъ, и достоѧ́нїю твоемꙋ̀: и ста́ни мл҃твенница къ ро́ждшемꙋся и́зъ тебѐ Бг҃ꙋ на́шемꙋ, да помо́жетъ на́мъ коне́чнw погиба́ющымъ, да и́зметъ ны̀ ѿ напа́стей неисцѣ́льныхъ. Зри́ши Влчⷭ҇це, коли́кими слеза́ми потопля́еми є́смы: ꙋми́лостивися ꙋ́бw, и не ѿри́ни на́съ до конца̀. Вскꙋ́ю Цр҃и́це лицѐ твоѐ ѿвраща́еши, забыва́еши нищетꙋ̀ на́шꙋ, и печа́ль на́шꙋ; Расточѝ належа́щїй на ны̀ стра́хъ и тре́петъ, ꙋтишѝ подви́гшїйся на ны̀ гнѣ́въ Бж҃їй, и па́гꙋбꙋ ꙋкротѝ, и сꙋ́щыя посредѣ̀ на́съ ра́спри и мяте́жи ꙋмирѝ, и тишинꙋ̀ и ми́ръ пода́ждь рабѡ́мъ твои̑мъ, да ко мно́гимъ твои̑мъ, бл҃годѣя́нїемъ, и сїя̑ приложи́вше, проповѣ́даемъ всегда̀ твоя̑ чꙋдеса̀. И до здѣ̀ доплы́вше, вѣ́трила словесѐ спꙋсти́вше, въ тве́рдомъ приста́нищи молча́нїя приста́немъ. Ѡ́но па́ки собра́вшымся воспомина́вше, да не неразꙋ́мни ꙗви́мся ѡ бл҃годѣя́нїи Влчⷭ҇цы: нижѐ дѣ́ломъ бл҃годѣ́йствꙋеми, лѣни́ви же словесы̀ бл҃годарє́нїе принесе́мъ: ꙗ́ко па́ки къ на́мъ прибы́токъ возврати́тся. А́ще бо ѡ прише́дшыхъ на ны̀ бл҃года́рни бꙋ́демъ, вели́кое себѣ̀ къ хотя́щымъ бы́ти ꙋгото́вимъ дерзнове́нїе, и неизрече́нныхъ бла́гъ полꙋчи́мъ, бл҃года́тїю и человѣколю́бїемъ Гдⷭ҇а на́шегw Іи҃са Хрⷭ҇та̀: ємꙋ́же сла́ва и держа́ва, че́сть и поклоне́нїе, ны́нѣ и при́снw, и во вѣ́ки вѣкѡ́въ, ами́нь.
items.english_text: Yet once again, because their violence was exalted into greatness on every side, it increased from the east unto the west and grew into a multitude.[^1413] And first indeed they entered into the Persian kingdom; and from thence into Egypt and Libya, giving their word to the Christians that they would not cause them to transgress the orthodox and blameless faith in Christ our God—which promise they did not keep, but showed forth many martyrs, because they refused to trample upon the Precious Cross, for this they compelled the Christians to do. And so to speak, they encompassed the whole earth with captivity, having overrun India, Ethiopia, Spain, the lands of the Moors, and Libya.

items.english_text: Last of all, they encamped against that very imperial city, desiring to take it. The Emperor being then the Isaurian, who had received the imperial crown, promised to pay them tribute. They, however, demanded that their own garrison be placed over the city; for they relied upon the multitude of their own troops and mercenaries, and upon the preparation of countless warriors in ships, the number of the vessels being one thousand and eight hundred, as those who have labored over chronicles have recorded.

items.english_text: These errant fighters against Christ placed their tents before the city; yet they brought not a single assault against the walls, for they were occupied in building houses, imagining that they would dwell there as at home, having woven such plans in their mind and intent, while the Lord frustrated their counsels. Meanwhile, the Christ-loving people within the city unceasingly celebrated the divine services, as was their custom to do, in peace and good order. Then taking up the all-venerable Wood of the Cross of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and the holy Icons of the Most Pure Mother of God, they walked—

Furthermore, their herald, having climbed a tall tree to proclaim their impure prayer, likewise fell down and wretchedly cast forth his godless soul.

Contending against them, he was defeated by them; and more than twenty thousand of his troops fell, while the survivors returned in shame unto their own.[^1415]

items.english_text: Having returned from the Bulgars, they attempted to reach the region of Blachernae with the ships they had brought. The stretching of iron chains from the imperial city unto Galata, however, prevented them, so that they were unable to accomplish what they had planned.[^1416] Sailing therefore as far as the place called Sosthenion and into other small harbors, the greater part of them were crushed and broken by a severe winter and dreadful winds; and the Greeks burned a multitude of other great ships.

items.english_text: Now the city was under great duress from the scarcity of human necessities. The adversaries, however, consumed without restraint whatever fell into their hands; and falling into a bitter extremity of famine, they were reduced even to tasting human flesh and the carcasses of unclean beasts, mingling unclean substances in their desperation. By reason of such desperate affliction, many of their notable and valiant men fled to the city and surrendered.[^1417]

items.english_text: For as of old He drowned the Egyptians who pursued Israel in the depths like a stone and brought the waters of the sea upon them, so also the Lord brought destruction upon the Saracens fleeing from the imperial city: for stirring up the sea with a dark wind and a dreadful, fiery tempest, He destroyed those thousands of ships. For while the majority of the vessels were sailing upon the Aegean deep, hail suddenly fell from heaven; and just as cold iron when brought near to fire boils up, so also the hailstones falling into the seawater caused it immediately to boil up. And by such boiling it melted the pitch of the opposing ships, and all sank into the depths, only three remaining to bring the report.[^1418]

items.english_text: Having reached this point in my discourse, and gazing up unto the height of the surpassing miracles of God and the Sovereign Lord, and of the unique Most Pure Theotokos, I become speechless with amazement, and I find no words worthy of these deeds. For what eloquent tongue can worthily praise the Virgin Theotokos? Or how can anyone gloriously hymn her glorious grace, to glorify the fountain of the love of mankind and to offer thanksgiving?

items.english_text: For it was fitting for us to offer thanksgiving unto the Mother of God by our deeds; for she herself and her Son rejoice far more in such deeds than in pipes, organs, and musical songs. And this is, as the Apostle also said: love without hypocrisy, which is the head of the Law and the Prophets; unswerving brotherly love; unrelenting compassion; divine virginity; lawful marriage; unsearchable chastity; conjoined righteousness; lawful courage against the passions; a God-directed understanding; inoffensive mercy; temperance without pride; well-contrite humility; and in addition to these, a blameless life, an upright character, a humble disposition, a prudent mind, God-proclaiming lips, a God-praising tongue, an unadulterous eye, hands free from plunder, feet not swift unto evil, an anger that is not unreasonable, subduing the fiery arrows of passionate thoughts; and all the other virtues whereby man, created according to the image of God and joined unto God, is adorned as with precious and beautiful raiment.[^1420]

items.season_or_tone: LENTEN OKTOECHOS SUPPLEMENT: TRINITY HYMNS AND COMPUNCTIVE STICHERA
items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: With such virtues ought we to give thanks unto God; for the wise have said that thanksgiving is composed of deeds and not of words alone. Yet since the weakness of our nature and the sluggishness of our mind make us slothful in virtuous labor, and we touch upon virtue only sparingly, as it were with the tip of our finger; for this reason we fall short in offering our due thanksgiving, so that we may at least offer songs in words.

items.section: At the Aposticha, Stichera for the Departed, Tone 8, Podoben: "O most marvelous wonder" (Ѽ пресла́внагѡ чꙋдесѐ)
items.season_or_tone: LENTEN OKTOECHOS SUPPLEMENT: TRINITY HYMNS AND COMPUNCTIVE STICHERA
items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: Thou, O Sovereign Lady Theotokos, possessing love for mankind by nature, hast not forsaken our Christian race, defending us as a mother who loves her children and is compassionate. Thus Thou dost ever grant Thy benefactions unto us, saving, covering, and preserving us, delivering us from perils and turning away tribulations. Therefore we give thanks for these things, and we proclaim Thy grace; we hide not Thy benefactions; we chant Thy miracles with a loud voice; we glorify Thine aid; we magnify Thy providence; we hymn Thy protection; we possess Thee as our beneficent helper; we glorify Thy tender mercy, and we remember Thy many great gifts, and from how many perils we have been delivered by Thee!

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: These songs of thanksgiving we offer unto Thee as a debt, not as though they were worthy of Thy benefaction, but rather as the lisping of smiling children. And concerning the present evils that afflict us, we implore Thy speedy aid; we have need of Thy protection: resolve the stumbling-blocks that exist in our midst! Dispel the cloud and darkness that encompass us, through which, as in a nocturnal battle, we are wounded—or rather to say, as though mad, we consume our own flesh, not understanding our kinship and not considering our common brotherhood, so that some among us dare to do such things, having been made worthy of that same Spirit, of the one Christ, of the same faith, of the same baptism, of the one Church, and of the same Mysteries!

items.english_text: Yet let us not extend our discourse further. For this reason we pray, O all-holy Sovereign Lady, unto Thy compassionate heart, that Thy mercies may be received by Thy people and Thine inheritance: and stand Thou as an intercessor before God Who was born of Thee, that He may help us who are perishing utterly, that He may deliver us from incurable misfortunes!

items.office: A Beneficial Tale Concerning the Akathist Hymn
items.section: At the Aposticha, Stichera for the Departed, Tone 8, Podoben: "O most marvelous wonder" (Ѽ пресла́внагѡ чꙋдесѐ)
items.season_or_tone: LENTEN OKTOECHOS SUPPLEMENT: TRINITY HYMNS AND COMPUNCTIVE STICHERA
items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: Thou seest, O Sovereign Lady, with how many tears we are inundated: have mercy therefore, and cast us not off unto the end! Why, O Queen, dost Thou turn Thy face away, and forget our poverty and our affliction? Scatter the fear and trembling that lie upon us; quiet the wrath of God that hath been stirred up against us; subdue destruction; make peace among the strife and turmoil that exist in our midst; and grant tranquility and peace unto Thy servants, that having added these also unto Thy many benefactions, we may ever proclaim Thy miracles!

items.english_text: And having sailed thus far, let us lower the sails of our discourse, and anchor in the firm haven of silence.[^1421] Calling these things again to the remembrance of those assembled, let us not appear ungrateful concerning the benefaction of the Sovereign Lady, nor, having been benefited in deed, let us be slothful in offering thanksgiving in words; so that an increase of blessing may return unto us again. For if we are thankful for the benefits that have come upon us, we shall prepare for ourselves great boldness toward those things that are to come, and we shall obtain unutterable blessings, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, unto Whom be glory and dominion, honor and worship, now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

For if we are thankful for the benefits that have come upon us, we shall prepare for ourselves great boldness toward those things that are to come, and we shall obtain unutterable blessings, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, unto Whom be glory and dominion, honor and worship, now and ever, and unto ages of ages. items.english_text: At the Divine Liturgy: the Beatitudes from the Canon of the Forefeast, Ode 3; and of the Martyr, Ode 6. After the Little Entrance, the troparia of the Forefeast, and of the temple of the Saint, and of the Martyr. Then the Kontakion of the temple of the Saint. *Glory:* of the Martyr. *Both now:* of the Forefeast. Prokeimenon, Epistle, Gospel, and Communion Hymn of the day and of the Saint.

items.section: At the Aposticha, Stichera for the Departed, Tone 8, Podoben: "O most marvelous wonder" (Ѽ пресла́внагѡ чꙋдесѐ)
items.season_or_tone: MARKIAN CHAPTERS
items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: At Small and Great Vespers, and at Matins, the entire service is celebrated as indicated for Cheesefare Monday, without change. At the end of Vespers and Matins, and of the Great Hour, there are 3 great prostrations. Only at the Hours do we say the troparia and Kontakion of the feast. At the Sixth Hour, the Troparion of the Prophecy is said, and the Prophecy is read. The Liturgy of John Chrysostom is celebrated at its proper time. We chant Vespers according to custom at its proper time. After the customary psalm, the kathisma of the day.

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: We do not say the kathisma; but after the customary psalm, we say: **"Lord, I have cried unto Thee"**. Then 8 stichera of the feast, and 3 of Saint Symeon. *Glory:* of the Saint. *Both now:* of the feast. Prokeimenon of the day, and the Prophecy. Then the prokeimenon: **"Let Israel hope in the Lord"**. At the Aposticha, the Idiomelon of the day from the Triodion, twice, and the Martyrikon. *Glory, both now:* of the feast. Troparion of the feast; and the dismissal.

items.english_text: At Great Vespers, we chant **"Blessed is the man"**, the first antiphon. At **"Lord, I have cried"**, we set 8 verses; and we chant 6 stichera of the feast, and 4 of the Fathers. *Glory:* of the Fathers. *Both now:* of the feast. Entrance. Prokeimenon of the day, and the readings of the feast. At Litiya, the stichera, and *Glory, both now:* of the feast. At the Aposticha, the stichera of the feast. *Glory:* of the Fathers. *Both now:* of the feast. At the Blessing of the Loaves, the Troparion of the feast, twice; and of the Fathers, once; and the reading of the feast.

items.day_or_date: On Friday of Palm Week, at Matins
items.english_text: We chant at Great Vespers all according to what is prescribed above: the Prokeimenon, the reading of the day, and the prokeimenon: **"Let Israel hope in the Lord"**. Then the readings of the feast. At the Aposticha of the feast; then the refrain of the Fathers: **"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His venerable ones"**; and we chant their Idiomelon: **"The multitudes of the monastics"**. *Glory:* the Idiomelon of the Triodion. *Both now:* of the feast.

items.english_text: At Matins, at **"God is the Lord"**, the Troparion of the feast, twice. *Glory:* of the Fathers. *Both now:* of the feast. After the Kathismata, the Sessional Hymns of the feast, and the reading of the feast. After the Polyeleos, the Sessional Hymn of the feast. Hymns of Ascent, the first antiphon of Tone 4; the Prokeimenon; **"Let every breath"**; the Gospel; and after Psalm 50, the sticheron of the feast.

At Ode 9, we chant **"More honorable"**; the Exapostilarion of the feast. *Glory:* of the Fathers. *Both now:* of the feast.

items.english_text: We do not say the verse of the Triodion; but after the stichera of the feast, we say *Glory:* of the Triodion; *Both now:* **"Most blessed art thou"**. Great Doxology. items.english_text: We chant the Canon of the feast with its Heirmos to 4; and of the Menaion, 3 troparia to 2; and of the Triodion to 8. items.english_text: We chant Great Compline, beginning at **"When I called"**; at which we chant the first morning triode of the Triodion. After **"It is truly meet"** and after the Trisagion, the Kontakion of the feast. After **"More honorable"**, 3 great prostrations; and at the dismissal, 3 prostrations. Likewise at the Midnight Office, after **"More honorable"**, 3 great prostrations.

Troparion of the Fathers. *Glory, both now:* of the feast; the litany; and the dismissal. At Compline, the Kontakion of the feast.

items.english_text: Canon of the feast with its Heirmos to 6, and of the Fathers to 8. Katavasia of the feast. The Exapostilarion of the Fathers. *Glory, both now:* of the feast.
